stewart_read: A $300/month bill is a strong pain anchor and the setter reacted well in the moment, but the call never got the chance to use it since the credit DQ arrived one exchange later.

quote: Okay. I know how much it is. And if that's a part of it, my credit is not good, and I won't be able to, like, get a loan for this at all.
stewart_read: The customer is mid-disclosure of a severe financial hardship (a $15,000 surprise tax bill, threatened forced sale of his home of 17 years) and is essentially narrating his own disqualification in real time. The setter does not interject with any acknowledgment during this stretch.

quote: Yeah. I'm sorry about that. Yeah. I tried to investigate it a little bit, but it couldn't get real far. So whatever.

But the schema is explicit that vulnerability disclosure is a trust-gift regardless of deal outcome — the customer's experience of the call still matters for brand perception.
coaching_implication: Even on a call ending in DQ, coach the rep to close with a fuller, more human acknowledgment rather than a clipped apology sandwiched into the DQ confirmation.

stewart_read: The customer volunteers a neighbor-influence reason for interest (garbled transcription but clearly referencing seeing a neighbor's solar install) unprompted. This is a strong, usable interest anchor that the setter never returns to or reinforces later in the call.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the call ends in a hard DQ within 4 minutes, there may have been no opportunity to circle back — the reactive read (setter simply ran out of runway) is well supported here since the credit gate ended the call almost immediately after.

Still worth flagging that when a customer gives a strong social-proof reason like a neighbor's system, reflecting it back ('oh so you've already seen one in action') builds trust even on calls likely to DQ.
